newsitem.title: USA: Whiskey bottles, jugs sought by collectors.
newsitem.headline: Whiskey bottles, jugs sought by collectors.

text.p: Monks in 11th century England were among the first to make it. Commercial production started 500 years later, about the time it was catching on in the New World.
But wherever it was distilled, whiskey had to be lugged and poured before drinking, and bottles, jugs and glasses have become sought after by a growing number of collectors.

Old whiskey vessels can make ideal gifts for the holidays. Many antique bottles, glasses or jugs can be had for modest amounts, but rare older varieties have been rising steadily in price, collectors and dealers say.
"This world is full of treasure-hunting stories," said John Goetz of Cedar Ridge Calif., who started collecting old bottles 15 years ago. "They're artifacts from early California history."

During the Gold Rush that started in 1848, thousands of miners tossed their empty whiskey bottles without a thought. About 30 years ago, people interested in the abandoned mining towns of northern California started digging up old trash heaps, helping bottle collecting come into its own.
Goetz said U.S.-made whiskey bottles fall into two main categories: historical flasks, made in the East, and western bottles produced from about 1870 onward.
Historical flasks are usually older and there are more types since more manufacturers were in the East, said Goetz, who has about 40 western bottles in his collection.
Goetz made quite a find last summer while poking around a second-hand store when he saw an old bottle in a wine rack.
"Most people just looked at it and saw a whiskey bottle. I knew it was rare, and figured it was worth at least $500," said Goetz, whose job is caring for disabled youngsters.

After doing some research, he found that a similar bottle from the western distiller Choice Old Cabinet had sold for $1,500 in 1995. That sort of find helps make collecting rewarding, the 50-year-old Goetz said.

Hot now are bottles from Bitters, a "medicine" that was produced mainly as a way around alcohol taxes, and bottles from Udolpho Wolfes, a New York-based company that marketed Dutch schnapps in the United States, Goetz said.
The rarest of Bitters bottles, especially in unusual colours, can fetch thousands of dollars, he said.

Udolpho Wolfes items are more modestly priced. Since the company sold millions of bottles of schnapps, most bottles are worth only $10 or $15, but some in rare colours such as purple can bring $300 or more, he said.

Look for square bottles embossed with the Udolpho Wolfes name on one side, and Aromatic Schnapps and Schiedam, a town in the Netherlands, on the other sides. The fourth side was left blank for a paper label.

Tom Duhn got interested in collecting whiskey jugs -- made for bar use to promote manufacturers' brands -- about a decade ago when his father-in-law gave him a Teachers jug. A Scotch fan at the time, he added a Dewars jug from an antique store.
"That's more or less how I started," said Duhn, who now has a collection of 550 jugs, most of them Scotch.

The jugs, made by distillers and used by bartenders to serve water, are usually ceramic, though some are glass or pewter. The earliest ones date from the turn of the century, and manufacturers still make them as promotional items.

Prices have been edging up and the rarest now fetch a few hundred dollars, said Duhn, founder of the Whisky Pitcher Collectors Association of America. (The spelling whisky is used for the drink made in Scotland from malted barley, as opposed to whiskeys made from other grains).

For instance, a Dewars jug made by Britain's Royal Doulton that sold for $300 last year could bring about 10 percent more now, Duhn estimated. The association's next annual convention is to be held in Bradenton, Fla., in May.
Interest has also been growing in old shot and beer glasses etched with the name of the distiller or brewer, said Pete Kroll, 49, a dealer and auctioneer in Wisconsin.

"Now all of a sudden there's more interest, and prices are going up," he said. Even common etched brewery glasses, each about three inches tall, will bring $40 or $50, up from $25 or $30 several years ago, while rarer ones sell for $200 or $300.

An enamel-coated beer glass from the Anaconda Brewing Co. in Montana is worth about $1,000, he said. "Fewer than 50 breweries made that kind of glass, mostly from late 1800s, and they typically sell for quite a bit," Kroll said.

Glasses from obscure distillers or brewers are hot. A glass from Northern Brewing Co. sold for $300 at a mail auction last month and one from Foxhead 400, another defunct Wisconsin brewery, brought $660, he said.
For more information, contact Kroll through Glasses, Mugs & Steins Auction at P.O. Box 207, Sun Prairie, Wis. 53590.
Membership in the Whisky Pitcher Collectors Association is $15 a year. It costs $35 to receive the colour newsletter. Call 847-566-9512 or e-mail Duhn at (thdpubjug1"at"aol.com).

Goetz said bottle shows across the country are a great place to learn. Most of them are free or charge a few dollars admission. Check libraries or local antique stores for references to shows or more information.
